newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock indices end up despite crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China stock indices end up despite crackdown.

text.p: China's share indices closed sharply higher on Friday despite a slew of announcements on punishment of major financial firms for illegal share trading.
Rumours of the measures had swirled around the markets for weeks, and brokers said the news had basically been digested by the time it emerged.
In Shanghai, the domestic A share index gained 33.084 points or 2.61 percent to 1,298.922, while the foreign currency B share index added 1.013 points or 1.22 percent to 83.931.
In Shenzhen, the A share index powered up 18.18 points or 4.40 percent to 431.09 after opening down 5.67 percent. The B share index gained 2.84 points or 1.98 percent to 146.16.
"Investors bought on the feeling that the bulk of rumoured bad news has come out," Peter Ho, an analyst at PBI Securities (Hong Kong) in Shenzhen, said.
But a securities analyst in Shanghai said this was not the end of the crackdown.
"The government has made it clear that they have the means to control the markets, and if it gets out of hand again, they will be used," he said.
China's regulators on Thursday announced punishments for a string of major listed firms and brokerages including Shenzhen Development Bank Co and Shenyin & Wanguo Securities for illegal share trades.
It was the latest in a series of measures imposed by Beijing since early May to cool down the volatile markets, including banning state banks from engaging in stock trading.
Brokers said the indices were also boosted today by rumours that the central bank would shortly cut bank reserve ratios. Officials declined to comment.

The Shenzhen Stock Exchange suspended trading in the country's only domestically listed bank, heavily index-weighted Shenzhen Development Bank, after Beijing punished the firm for illegally trading its own shares.
Traders said the suspension of the bank rescued the markets, especially the A share index, from a nosedive early in the morning.
"The suspension shows that the authorities want to regulate the market rather than kill it," a trader at China Guotai Securities said.
Despite the day's rise, brokers said market sentiment was unstable and many investors were still worried Beijing would take further measures to cool down stock trading.

"Many believe that if the indices rise firmly again, the central government will take further crackdown measures," a Shanghai broker said. "The market lacks the momentum to rise further next week with sentiment still cautious."
"I don't think the shares will rebound sharply next week as there are still rumours of more anti-speculation measures," said a Shenzhen-based analyst at China Securities Co.

Shanghai Jinqiao Export Processing Zone Development Co was the most actively traded B share and the biggest gainer on the Shanghai A share market, rising $0.054 or 6.71 percent to $0.858 on volume of 2.5 million shares.
In Shenzhen, the biggest B share gainer was Chiwan Wharf Holdings which rose HK$0.45 or 9.18 percent to HK$5.35.
